titleEn: Happy is the one who considers the weak
progression: | Dm Dm | Gm Gm | Dm A7 | Dm Dm |
intro: Fourteen verses, and one of the psalms people say at a sickbed. It opens with a rule stated about somebody else, that whoever attends to the weak is attended to in his own weak hour, and then the speaker turns out to be the weak one: from verse 5 he is in bed, his visitors are counting the days, and the friend who ate at his table has turned on him. For a learner the drill is the third person object suffix, four verbs carrying it in verses 2 to 4 alone. Verse 14 is not part of the poem. It is the doxology that closes Book One of the Psalms, and the same formula ends each of the other four books.

stichs.en: For the choirmaster.
A psalm of David.

verses.summary: A performance heading rather than a line of the prayer. The first word is usually taken as the person responsible for the music, which marks this as a psalm handed over to be sung.

stichs.en: Happy is the one who gives thought to the weak;
on a day of evil the LORD will deliver him.

verses.summary: The psalm opens with a rule about a third party, not with a request. Its logic is reciprocal: the treatment given to the weak is the treatment received on the bad day.

stichs.en: The LORD will keep him and keep him alive; he shall be called happy in the land,
and do not give him over to the appetite of his enemies.

glosses: and he shall be called happy
verses.summary: The rule is spelled out as things God will do, and then the grammar slips into petition with a negative command. That slip is the first sign the speaker has himself in mind.

stichs.en: The LORD will sustain him on the couch of illness;
all his bed You have turned in his sickness.

verses.summary: The sickbed arrives, and with it the first second person verb in the psalm. The rule has stopped being general and is now being addressed to someone.

stichs.en: As for me, I said:
O LORD, be gracious to me, heal my soul,
for I have sinned against You.

verses.summary: The first person takes over for the rest of the psalm. The request for healing is filed together with an admission of guilt, which makes the illness and the sin one case rather than two.

stichs.en: My enemies say evil of me:
When will he die and his name perish?

verses.summary: The enemies are given their own speech. What they are waiting for is not his defeat but his erasure, the name going with the man.

stichs.en: And if one comes to see me, he speaks emptiness;
his heart gathers wickedness for itself;
he goes outside and tells it.

verses.summary: The visitor is the worst of them. The verse follows him from the door to the street, and the same verb for speaking frames both ends: empty words inside, and outside the real report.

stichs.en: All who hate me whisper together against me;
against me they devise harm for me.

verses.summary: The whispering is collective, and the direction is stated twice in one verse. The speaker is hearing his own case being discussed while he lies there.

stichs.en: A thing of worthlessness is poured into him;
now that he lies down, he will not rise again.

verses.summary: Their verdict, quoted. They read the illness as a judgement poured into him, which is the same theology the speaker used about himself in verse 5, here turned into a weapon.

stichs.en: Even the man of my peace,
in whom I trusted,
who eats my bread,
has made his heel great against me.

verses.summary: The betrayal comes last because it is the worst: not an enemy but a table companion. Peace, trust, bread, heel is the whole friendship and its end in four words.

stichs.en: But You, O LORD, be gracious to me,
and raise me up, that I may repay them.

verses.summary: The turn. What he asks for is exactly what the rule of verse 2 promised, and he asks for it as a case being brought rather than as a favour being begged.

stichs.en: By this I know that You have delighted in me:
that my enemy does not shout in triumph over me.

verses.summary: The proof he offers is negative. Not that he has been healed, but that nobody is celebrating yet. Confidence here is measured by what has failed to happen.

stichs.en: And as for me, You have upheld me in my integrity,
and set me before You forever.

verses.summary: The claim of integrity answers the confession of verse 5 without cancelling it. Held up and set in place are both things done to him; he does neither of them himself.

stichs.en: Blessed is the LORD, the God of Israel,
from everlasting to everlasting.
Amen and amen.

verses.summary: Not part of the poem. This is the doxology that closes Book One of the Psalms, and the doubled amen is a reader's signature at the end of a section.

pardes.body: Three movements and a seal. Verses 2 to 4 state a principle in the third person: the one who attends to the weak is attended to in his turn. Verses 5 to 11 are the speaker's own case, in the first person, from a bed, with a visitor who comes to look, whispering behind his back, and a friend who ate his bread. Verses 12 and 13 close with the evidence he is willing to accept, which is only that the enemy has not yet won. Verse 14 stands outside all of it as the doxology ending Book One of the Psalms. Read whole, the psalm is a man testing his own opening line on himself and finding it holds, barely.

One noun carries the psalm twice. {{3.7}} asks that he not be handed over to the nefesh of his enemies, where the word means appetite or the throat that swallows, and {{5.5}} asks for healing of nafshi, the same noun used for the self that is sick. Biblical Hebrew gives that word both jobs, and this psalm puts them two verses apart. {{4.7}} is the crux: a second person verb meaning You have turned, arriving without warning in a line otherwise about God in the third person, with an object that is either his bed or his lying down. Whether the sense is that the bed was turned in nursing him, or that the sickness itself was turned into health, is disputed, and translations split on it. {{10.10}} is an idiom found nowhere else in the Bible, literally he made the heel great against me. Every English version guesses, and lifted his heel is a guess.

Verse 4 became the text behind visiting the sick. If the sustaining happens at the bed itself, then the bed is where a person should be, and a visitor who arrives there is doing a small version of what the verse describes. That reading also explains why the psalm is said at sickbeds rather than only said about them. Verse 10 is usually read against the books of Samuel, where David's own counsellor goes over to Absalom, and the phrase the man of my peace is taken as naming him without naming him. The identification is not forced by the text, and the psalm never gives a name, which is part of why it stays usable by anyone betrayed by someone closer than an enemy.

The shape of the psalm is a measure coming back. What is given at the top, attention paid to someone with no power, returns at the bottom, when the giver has no power either, and the traditional name for that symmetry is measure for measure. {{13.4}} is the end point: a verb meaning to set upright and station, with the speaker as its object and before Your face as its place, forever. Nothing is said about the illness being cured. What changes is where he stands, and in the mystical idiom that is the whole of what a person can ask for: not the removal of the condition but a fixed position in front of the source.
